Name: 4-bit core
Description: A minimal 4-bit processor core for calculators and controllers.

Name: 8-bit core
Description: An 8-bit processor core. Twice the work per clock, but a longer critical path.

Name: Enhanced 8-bit core
Description: A refined 8-bit core with a richer instruction set and faster decode.

Name: 16-bit core
Description: A 16-bit core with a wide datapath. Home computers and workstations want it.

Name: 32-bit core
Description: A 32-bit core with pipelining. Big, power-hungry and very fast.

Name: On-chip RAM, 64 B
Description: Scratch RAM beside the core. No spare rows, so any defect in it kills the die.

Name: On-chip RAM, 256 B
Description: Larger RAM with one spare row that can repair a single defect.

Name: Cache, 1 KB
Description: An instruction and data cache. Spare rows repair up to two defects.

Name: Cache, 4 KB
Description: A large cache. Most of its area is repairable SRAM.

Name: Mask ROM, 512 B
Description: Program storage fixed at manufacture. Calculators and controllers need it.

Name: Mask ROM, 2 KB
Description: Room for a full program or a character set.

Name: Memory interface
Description: A narrow multiplexed bus to external memory.

Name: DRAM controller
Description: Drives DRAM directly, with refresh. Cuts board cost for customers.

Name: 16-bit bus interface
Description: A wide bus that keeps a 16-bit core fed.

Name: I/O ring, 16 pads
Description: Bond pads and drivers. Must sit on the die edge.

Name: I/O ring, 24 pads
Description: Bond pads and drivers for a 24-pin part. Must sit on the die edge.

Name: I/O ring, 40 pads
Description: Bond pads and drivers for a 40-pin part. Must sit on the die edge.

Name: I/O ring, 64 pads
Description: Bond pads and drivers for a 64-pin part. Must sit on the die edge.

Name: I/O ring, 132 pads
Description: Bond pads and drivers for a pin-grid package. Must sit on the die edge.

Name: Video shifter
Description: Turns memory into a video signal. The simplest display hardware.

Name: Sprite engine
Description: Moves sprites over a background. Several on one die can be harvested if one fails.

Name: Tile and sprite processor
Description: Scrolling tile maps and many sprites. The heart of a games console.

Name: Keyboard scanner
Description: Scans a key matrix and debounces keys. Every calculator needs one.

Name: Display driver
Description: Drives LED or LCD digits directly, saving the customer a driver chip.

Name: Timers
Description: Counters that run while the core does other work. Controllers lean on them.

Name: Interrupt controller
Description: Lets devices interrupt the core instead of being polled.

Name: Serial port
Description: A UART for terminals, modems and printers.

Name: Hardware multiplier
Description: Multiplies in a few clocks instead of dozens. Sits right beside the core.

Name: A/D converter
Description: Reads sensors directly. Analog circuitry barely shrinks with the process.

Name: DMA controller
Description: Moves data to and from memory without the core, freeing bus time.

Name: Prefetch queue
Description: Fetches instructions ahead of the core so it waits less on memory. Must sit next to the core.

Name: Sound generator
Description: Tone and noise channels. Games consoles and home computers want them.

Name: Floating-point unit
Description: Hardware floating point. Big and slow-pathed, but a defect in it only switches it off: sell those dies without an FPU.

Name: Memory management unit
Description: Virtual memory and protection for multi-tasking systems.
